A. HISTORY OF THE SOFTWARE
==========================

Python was created in the early 1990s by Guido van Rossum at Stichting
Mathematisch Centrum (CWI, see https://www.cwi.nl) in the Netherlands
as a successor of a language called ABC.  Guido remains Python's
principal author, although it includes many contributions from others.

In 1995, Guido continued his work on Python at the Corporation for
National Research Initiatives (CNRI, see https://www.cnri.reston.va.us)
in Reston, Virginia where he released several versions of the
software.

In May 2000, Guido and the Python core development team moved to
BeOpen.com to form the BeOpen PythonLabs team.  In October of the same
year, the PythonLabs team moved to Digital Creations, which became
Zope Corporation.  In 2001, the Python Software Foundation (PSF, see
https://www.python.org/psf/) was formed, a non-profit organization
created specifically to own Python-related Intellectual Property.
Zope Corporation was a sponsoring member of the PSF.

All Python releases are Open Source (see https://opensource.org for
the Open Source Definition).  Historically, most, but not all, Python

/******************************************************************************
** This file is an amalgamation of many separate C source files from SQLite
** version 3.53.1.  By combining all the individual C code files into this
** single large file, the entire code can be compiled as a single translation
** unit.  This allows many compilers to do optimizations that would not be
** possible if the files were compiled separately.  Performance improvements
** of 5% or more are commonly seen when SQLite is compiled as a single
** translation unit.
**
** This file is all you need to compile SQLite.  To use SQLite in other
** programs, you need this file and the "sqlite3.h" header file that defines
** the programming interface to the SQLite library.  (If you do not have
** the "sqlite3.h" header file at hand, you will find a copy embedded within
** the text of this file.  Search for "Begin file sqlite3.h" to find the start
** of the embedded sqlite3.h header file.) Additional code files may be needed
** if you want a wrapper to interface SQLite with your choice of programming
** language. The code for the "sqlite3" command-line shell is also in a
** separate file. This file contains only code for the core SQLite library.
**
** The content in this amalgamation comes from Fossil check-in

Python navigation accompanying materials and repackaging summary

Mirket 0.0.1 selects unchanged CPython 3.13.17 normal-GIL files from
python-build-standalone release 20261021, source recipe commit
0c5e581b54a4736cdbbe68bdd6d7e571a1dca11e. Mirket changes file selection and
private installed permissions only. It omits package/environment managers,
Tcl/Tk/GUI facilities, most development headers/build helpers, and upstream
fixture/bytecode material. It adds original notices and this summary. Mirket
has not changed or rebuilt the selected interpreter, libpython or stdlib bytes.
The complete retained/omitted selection is recorded in m3-python-macos.selection.json.
The upstream build has its own CPython patches; its complete pinned recipe and
patch sources accompany this payload under sources/python-general. These are
inert source archives, available for inspection and modification under their
original terms; no build helper is invoked by Mirket. The MPL-2.0 license for
python-build-standalone is preserved in upstream/python-build-standalone-LICENSE.txt.

Jedi 0.20.1 and parso 0.8.7 wheels are unchanged upstream artifacts; no extras
are selected. Their complete unchanged source distributions accompany this
payload under sources/python-navigation. Jedi includes vendored typeshed
(Apache-2.0 plus MIT) and django-stubs (MIT) data. parso includes PSF-licensed
stdlib-derived files and MIT contributions. Their original AUTHORS and LICENSE
files remain inside the unchanged wheels and are copied separately here.
Upstream inline copyright/license text remains in the full source archives.
No third-party component is relicensed as Mirket-authored MIT code.

The native runtime links macOS system libraries/frameworks that are supplied
by the OS. They are not copied into this payload. The exact source archives for
CPython and the bundled native components accompany this payload under
sources/python-general, with their original per-file terms. Full source archives
include build/test/other-platform material that is not part of the selected
runtime. Their presence is not an added executable capability. The standalone
build license copies for bzip2 and libffi are retained for provenance; additional
source-authentic license copies here preserve the newer copyright attribution.

Use the explicit release-owned interpreter with -I -S -B. The release does not
select Python, Jedi, parso or their data from PATH, user/site packages or a project,
and it does not fetch or install anything on first use. Runtime paths and wheel
bytes are exact release inventory entries. This package is a private host process,
not an OS sandbox. Platform qualification and capability coverage are reported
separately from these source and notice materials.
